article.overview:
Lunar regolith is an abrasive material. Its grains are sharp and irregular, and its fine dust is easily disturbed and can cling to and grind surfaces. An abrasion tester measures this effect in a controlled way. A sample is worn against a standard abrasive, and the amount of material lost is recorded [2][3]. Such a device could in principle be flown to measure wear on the Moon, or to prepare rock surfaces for analysis, but no flown lunar abrasion tester was identified in the sources read for this article.

Current work is mainly on the ground. NASA Langley and its collaborators have used Taber-style abrasive wheels made from lunar regolith simulant and compared them with standard ceramic abrasives. They report different wear rates [2]. A NASA Langley testbed for lunar wear tests under vacuum was described in 2024 [1]. Abrasion tools that grind rock surfaces form a separate, flown heritage. The Rock Abrasion Tool on NASA's Mars Exploration Rovers ground a shallow patch in a Martian rock in 2004 [5]. That tool was built to remove weathered rock surfaces, not to measure wear.
article.description: An abrasion tester brings a sample into controlled contact with an abrasive, usually under a defined load and for a set number of cycles. It then measures the loss of material or the change in the surface. Wear is normally reported as mass or volume lost over a set number of cycles, although the exact method depends on the standard being followed. The sources describe two broad uses. Materials testing: an abrasive wheel or tumbler is run against a candidate material, such as a spacesuit fabric or a coating, to measure how fast lunar dust would wear it [2][3]. Rock surface preparation: a rotating grinding bit cuts a small, shallow, roughly circular patch so that the fresh interior of a rock can be seen. The Mars Rock Abrasion Tool did this [5]. The regolith-based wheels in the 2025 work are test abrasives, not sensors. They are used to make wear measurements more representative of the lunar case [2].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Abrasion testers serve three purposes in the sources read. They measure how fast candidate lunar hardware, such as fabrics, coatings and moving mechanisms, wears under a realistic abrasive [1][2][3]. They help assess dust-mitigation methods over long periods; the 2025 abstract argues that this is one of the applications for regolith-based abrasives [2]. For rock abrasion tools, they prepare a fresh surface so that other instruments can analyse the rock's interior, as the Mars Rock Abrasion Tool did [5]. The 2025 abstract argues that regolith-based abrasives represent two-body abrasion between materials and lunar dust better than standard ceramic abrasives do [2]. That is a claim about test realism, not a measured performance result.
article.operating_principle: In materials testing, a sample and a standard abrasive wheel or tumbler move against each other under controlled load and for a set number of cycles. The material lost is measured by weight or volume, and comparing abrasives gives a wear ranking. The 2023 study used three abrasion methods on sieved lunar simulant and spacesuit fabric: a rotary tumbler, the Martindale method and an Accelerotor. It compared coated and uncoated fabric [3]. In rock abrasion, a rotating grinding bit is pressed against the rock and cuts a shallow, roughly circular hole. Loose dust is then cleared so that the fresh surface can be inspected [5]. Secondary sources describe a diamond-and-resin bit, but this was not confirmed on a primary source read for this article.
article.scientific_importance: Lunar dust is both abrasive and electrostatic. It was a major problem during Apollo, and it remains a concern for Artemis-era hardware [3]. Wear data for such hardware depend on the abrasive used. Regolith-based wheels offer one way to obtain more realistic data [2]. The value of any ground test is limited by how faithful the simulant is. The 2025 abstract does not name its simulant [2].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an abrasion tester. The examples differ in purpose and maturity: a test abrasive, a laboratory testbed and a flown rock-grinding tool. The sources read publish no mass, size or power values for the lunar-relevant examples, and the values for the flown Mars tool are not comparable with laboratory items. The examples should not be compared directly.

examples.name: Regolith-simulant Taber abrasive wheels
examples.abrasive_comparison: Regolith-based Taber wheels were tested against standard ceramic-based abrasives. The 2025 abstract reports a difference in wear rates, but does not say which material wears faster and gives no numbers [2].
examples.iac_2024_wheels: Standard CS-17 wheels compared with new wheels made from lunar mare simulant LMS-1 (Space Resource Technologies) for abrasion of Al6061-T6 aluminium samples [4].
examples.simulant_particle_size: Search-result summary of [4] gives mean particle size as greater than 60 µm. Unverified; full PDF not read.
examples.test_standard: Search-result summary of [4] says ASTM D4060. Unverified; full PDF not read.
examples.volumetric_loss_claim: A secondary summary of [2] claims an order-of-magnitude difference. Not confirmed by the abstract; not used.

examples.name: NASA Langley lunar extreme-environment wear testbed
examples.description: Reconfigurable testbed for rapid, repeatable wear testing of materials and candidate mechanisms under vacuum. Preliminary results are reported for an actuating mechanism similar to a pin joint, exposed to lunar regolith simulant under high vacuum.

examples.name: Rock Abrasion Tool (Mars Exploration Rovers)

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No lunar abrasion tester has published dimensions. The Langley testbed dimensions are not stated in the record [1]. The RAT grind patch is 45.5 mm across and 4.4 mm deep [5]. Those are the dimensions of the ground cut, not of the instrument.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not publicly specified for any lunar-relevant example. The source page for the RAT does not give mass [5].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified for the Langley testbed or for the lunar-relevant examples. Power values for the RAT conflict between secondary sources and are not used [5].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The lunar environment changes what an abrasion test means. Lunar dust is abrasive and electrostatic, so it can cling to and abrade surfaces [3]. The Langley testbed is designed for vacuum, which is representative of the lunar surface [1]. The lunar surface also has large temperature swings and no atmosphere. A flight tester would have to survive these conditions, but the sources read give no quantified environmental requirement for an abrasion tester.
article.limitations:
- Ground results depend on the simulant. Grain size, shape and chemistry control the wear. The 2025 abstract does not name its simulant [2]. The 2023 study found that larger grains were more abrasive than smaller ones, but the abstract gives no size values [3].
- In the 2023 controlled tests, the selected ceramic coatings did not reduce abrasion [3]. The authors recommend testing further coatings.
- Numerical results are scarce in the sources read. The full texts of [2] and [4] could not be read.
- The Rock Abrasion Tool is a Mars instrument. Its performance does not transfer directly to the Moon [5].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: No lunar abrasion tester has flown. A flight unit would be a surface instrument. Its transportation would need Earth integration, launch, lunar transfer, delivery by a lander, deployment by an arm or mechanism, and power, data, thermal and mechanical interfaces. The ground testbeds in Examples 1 and 2 are laboratory items and are not transported.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into a spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth.
Launch it using a launch vehicle.
Deliver it to the surface with a lunar lander.
Deploy it with an arm or mechanism, then connect power, data, thermal and mechanical interfaces.
If the tester handles regolith samples, sample-handling payloads 161 and 162 would be relevant.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not specified for any lunar abrasion tester. A flight unit would need a deployment method suited to its mass and the surface contact it must make.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Mars Exploration Rover Rock Abrasion Tool was deployed on the Martian surface on the Opportunity rover, where it made its first grind on sol 30 [5]. This is a Mars example, not a lunar one.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander has been assessed. No verified interface evidence was found in the sources read.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo missions showed that lunar dust is a serious engineering problem. The 2023 paper describes dust as highly abrasive and electrostatic, and notes that it was a major challenge during Apollo [3]. The Mars Rock Abrasion Tool provides a flown precedent for grinding a rock surface ahead of analysis. Its first grind on Opportunity took place on sol 30 of the mission, in February 2004 [5]. Recent NASA work on lunar-regolith wear testing, from 2023 to 2025, has used ground testbeds and regolith-based abrasives [1][2][4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- No flown lunar abrasion tester was identified in the sources read.
- Mass, size, power and sample-size values for lunar-relevant abrasion testers are not publicly specified in the sources read.
- The full text of [2] (a 2025 presentation) was not read. Its wear rates and methods are unverified.
- The PDF of [4] could not be read. The LMS-1 particle size and the ASTM D4060 method come only from a search-result summary.
- The PDF of [3] could not be read. The abstract page gives no grain size values.
- For the Rock Abrasion Tool, secondary sources conflict on depth and power. Only the NASA/JPL values are used. The diamond-and-resin bit description is secondary-source only.
- The general Apollo-era reporting of dust abrasion is not linked to a specific Apollo abrasion instrument. No such instrument was identified.
- One image is included. Its direct asset URL was taken from the source page and was not separately fetched. NASA media usage terms should be checked before republication.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: No flown lunar abrasion tester was identified. The payload name covers ground test devices and rock abrasion tools; the article treats both meanings and labels them.

The PDF of NASA NTRS record 20240012146 (IAC 2024) could not be read. The LMS-1 mean particle size (greater than 60 µm) and the ASTM D4060 method come only from a search-result summary and are unverified.
The PDF of NTRS record 20230000758 could not be read. The abstract page gives no grain size values, simulant name or numeric results.
The full presentation behind NTRS record 20250000687 was not read. Its wear rates, simulant name and wheel fabrication method are not given in the record page.
The secondary-source claim of an order-of-magnitude volumetric loss difference for regolith-simulant wheels was not confirmed and is not used.

For the Mars Rock Abrasion Tool, secondary sources conflict on grind depth and average power. Only the NASA/JPL values (45.5 mm patch, 4.4 mm deep, sol 30) are used. The diamond-and-resin bit description is secondary-source only.
The SLIDE apparatus name appears only in secondary search summaries and is not used as a fact.
The RAT image asset URL was taken from the NASA source page and was not separately fetched, so its availability is unchecked. The page does not label resolution.
